abstract: Aims: PD-1 signaling limits cardiac remodeling and heart failure (HF). Whether this protection depends on PD-1 signaling intrinsic to CD8 T cells or on regulation by other immune populations, including regulatory T cells (Tregs), remains unclear. Methods and results: Using transverse aortic constriction (TAC), we studied global PD-1-knockout (KO) mice with or without CD8 T cell depletion, CD8 T cell-specific (PD1KOCD8), and Treg-specific PD-1-KO mice. We assessed left ventricular (LV) remodeling, genomic profiles, immune infiltration, and the therapeutic impact of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3) blockade. CD8 T cell depletion abolished TAC-induced left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, fibrosis, and dysfunction of global PD-1-KO mice. PD1KOCD8 mice had normal baseline cardiac function but, after TAC, showed reduced survival, worse LV dysfunction and fibrosis, and greater immune cell infiltration. CD8 T cells from PD1KOCD8 mice showed increased activation and proliferation, with increased production of cytotoxic molecules, such as IFN-{gamma} and granzyme A, both at baseline and after TAC. Post-TAC transcriptomics revealed enhanced inflammatory pathways and suppressed metabolic pathways in PD1KOCD8 hearts. TAC also increased LV CXCR3+CD8+ T cell accumulation and CXCL9/CXCL10 expression in PD1KOCD8 mice. CXCR3 neutralizing antibody treatment reduced LV CD8+ T cell accumulation and attenuated cardiac dysfunction. In contrast, Treg-specific PD-1 deficiency did not alter baseline or TAC-induced cardiac remodeling. Conclusions: CD8 T cell-intrinsic PD-1 restrains TAC-induced HF, whereas Treg-intrinsic PD-1 is dispensable. CXCR3-dependent recruitment drives pathological CD8 T cell accumulation, identifying PD-1/CXCR3 axis as a key regulator of CD8 T cell-mediated cardiac injury.
